newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia slowing down on private power.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia slowing down on private power.

text.p: Malaysia, which now has a huge surplus of electrical power, may stop awarding new licences to independent power producers, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Monday.

"The number of (IPP) plants that are being started, or in the process of being approved is quite big, and I think we may have to call a halt at the moment," he told reporters after opening an electricity supply exhibition.
At present, Malaysia has a total installed capacity of 10,110 megawatts, and a peak demand of 7,063 megawatts -- a reserve margin of about 43 percent.

Mahathir also said he wanted to ensure the continued profitability of partly-privatised power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB). "We don't want to kill the national TNB in order to give a lot of profits to the IPPs."

Twelve independents have been awarded licenses so far and five of them are in operation. Together they provide 30 percent of peninsular Malaysia's electricity. The rest is produced by Tenaga, the copuntry's sole distributor of electricity.

Demand would be matched by new supply as and when it was needed, Mahathir said, before clambering into an electric go-kart and speeding around the car park outside the exhibit hall with Energy, Telecommunications and Post Minister Leo Moggie racing against him in another kart.
"The news appears to be very positive for Tenaga," said a power utility analyst at a foreign-based broking house in Kuala Lumpur.

"We will still need an IPP program, as Malaysia's electricity usage is currently growing by around 10 to 15 percent per annum. At this rate the reserve margin would only be around 30 or even 20 percent by the year 2000," he said.
"After 2000, we will need new capacity which could be satisfied by new IPPs or Tenaga itself," added the analyst.

Up until now, Tenaga has had to weather mostly bad news, including a nationwide blackout in August that Mahathir said was a national embarrassment. A British consultancy has since been hired to look at a possible revamp of the company.

Tenaga said last Wednesday it would be awarding rebates of 10 percent, spread over December 1996 and January 1997, to 4.2 million consumers as compensation for the blackout. The rebates will total 70 million ringgit
The company also took a blow last year, when a rate hike it had pushed hard for was rejected by the Cabinet.
Tenaga chairman Tajuddin Ali said recently he would not push for another rate hike until he was confident that he could tell the government the company was being run efficiently.
Tenaga had a monopoly in the power industry until five IPPs, amounting to 4,115 megawatts of generation capacity, were approved in 1993.
The IPPs represented 51 percent of the new capacity at the time of the awards, making Malaysia one of the fastest-growing power markets in the world.
In his speech opening the exhibition, Mahathir defended the use of hydro-electric power as environmentally friendly.

The 2,400 megawatt capacity Bakun dam, to be built in a Borneo rain forest, has been heavily criticised by environmentalists concerned that the dam would clear an area of rainforest the size of Singapore and displace 9,400 tribal residents.
"Of course, hydro-electric plants will change the character of vast tracts of land, possibly primal forest," Mahathir said.
"But these lands are also threatened by logging, clearing for agriculture, including shifting cultivation and human settlement eventually." ($1 = 2.50 ringgit)
